One Pile

Game StrategyNumber Theory

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: you and the computer take turns taking objects from one pile; when nobody can take any more, whoever took last wins.
How to play: press a number to take that many. It can be no smaller than Min and no bigger than Max. Changing Min or Max deals a new pile.
0

Look for the math

With no limit on how many you may take, a single pile is over in one move. Bound the take from below and above, and the game suddenly has a shape: some pile sizes are safe to leave, and some are not.

Losing piles

A pile is a losing position (a P-position) when every take leaves a winning pile for the other player. For One Pile those sizes are exactly the ones whose remainder on division by Min + Max is smaller than Min:

0 ≤ S mod (Min + Max) < Min

The logic test checks this against perfect play for every Min from 1 to 12 and every Max from Min to 45, over three full periods. It holds in every case, and it also holds in the applet's version, where a take may be bigger than the pile.

What the computer does

Write r = N mod (Min + Max). If r is already a losing remainder, the computer shrugs and takes at random. If Min ≤ r ≤ Max, it takes exactly r and leaves a multiple of the period. If r > Max, it picks a take that drops the remainder into [0, Min). That is the applet's MakeMove, ported as it is — including the quirk that a random take from a losing pile never rolls Max itself.

Grundy numbers

The same pattern shows up in the Grundy numbers (nimbers) of the pile. For Min = 3 and Max = 5 the page lists

0 0 0 1 1 1 2 2 and then it repeats.

The zeros fall exactly on the P-positions. The logic test recomputes the mex of each size up to 20 and matches the table.

What differs from the applet

The applet let a player take more than the pile held, and the pile then showed a negative number. Here a take can be no bigger than the pile. It changes nothing about who wins: when at least Min are left, taking exactly what is left already ends the game, and the logic test confirms that the winner from every pile is the same with or without the extra takes. You press a number where the applet had buttons round the edge of its picture. A finished game cannot be taken back, because the score has counted it, and the running score is new: the applet had none. Make move passes your turn, so the computer can go first, and works after Take back too.

Try Min = 3 and Max = 5 with a pile whose size mod 8 is 0, 1 or 2. Let the computer go first (Make move): can you still win?
